title: Genesis, looking back
hook: a garden, a rainbow, a ladder, a wrestling match, a brother forgiven
tomorrow: when Moses left Egypt, whose bones did he carry?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's list of everything that might come between, each one crossed out: nothing can separate us. Today, the Bible's first book, and a family that nearly tore itself apart.
screen: `NOTHING CAN SEPARATE US.` → `A FAMILY, NEARLY TORN.`

segments.voice: A rejection email that pushed someone toward the work they love. A fight that ended a friendship, and the apology years later that started a better one. People tell these stories carefully, because the hurt was real. Genesis ends on one. Their father has just died, and the brothers are afraid. Years ago they threw their younger brother into a pit and sold him. Now he rules in Egypt, and holds their lives in his hands.
screen: `A REJECTION, A FIGHT, A LATE APOLOGY.` → `THE HURT WAS REAL.` → `NOW HE HOLDS THEIR LIVES.`

segments.voice: Joseph answers: “Fear not: for am I in the place of God? But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.” Notice the order. He names the evil first. He doesn't call harm good. He sets something larger beside it. Look back over Genesis and that pattern keeps surfacing: a garden lost, and God still calling, “Where art thou?”; a flood, then a bow in the cloud, “a token of a covenant between me and the earth”; a runaway on a stone pillow who wakes and says, “Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.” Jews read these stories as Torah, Christians as the opening of their Bible. Now a neighbor. Muslims know this brother as Yusuf, and the Qur'an tells his story in the surah named for him. When his brothers stand before him at last, he says: “Have no fear this day! May Allah forgive you.” Here's one to tell a friend: in both books, the wronged brother's first words to the frightened ones are nearly the same, fear not. Shared ground: a brother who has the power to take revenge, and won't. An honest difference: the Qur'an honors Yusuf as a prophet, and its telling keeps turning to what God knows and plans; Genesis tells him as one son in a long, tangled family story.
screen: `HE NAMES THE EVIL FIRST.` · `A GARDEN, A BOW, A LADDER.` · `A NEIGHBOR: HAVE NO FEAR THIS DAY.` · `SHARED GROUND, HONEST DIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `MEANT FOR GOOD.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly for about a minute, around a room or down a hallway. Every few steps, let one Genesis picture pass: a garden, a rainbow, a ladder, a wrestling match, a brother forgiven. Notice where you stop; that may be your story. If you pray, sit afterward and pray from inside it.
Genesis. The Bible's first book: a garden, a rainbow, a ladder, a wrestling match, and a brother who names the harm and forgives.
Keep this: meant for good, with the harm named and the good set beside it. See you tomorrow.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3 (shape: wisdom: can harm be meant for good? Genesis's answer in Joseph, with one neighbor tradition). Title, word, carry and sources kept; Genesis 50:19 joined to the 50:20 quotation; Genesis 32:26 now paraphrased by mention only (the wrestling match); Qur'an 12:92 added.

Unity thread: the Qur'an's Yusuf (Surah 12) as the neighbor. Quoted from Pickthall 1930, Qur'an 12:92 ('He said: Have no fear this day! May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.'); confirm the wording word for word against Pickthall before release. Shared ground: the wronged brother refuses revenge and opens with nearly the same words ('Fear not', Genesis 50:19; 'Have no fear this day', Qur'an 12:92). Honest difference, ranking neither: the Qur'an honors Yusuf as a prophet and its telling keeps returning to God's knowledge and plan; Genesis tells him as one son within a long family story. Note the scenes differ: Genesis 50:19 is after Jacob's death; Qur'an 12:92 is when Yusuf makes himself known to his brothers. The lesson says 'when his brothers stand before him at last' for the Qur'an scene. Confirm a Muslim reader and a Jewish reader would find this fair. 'Jews read these stories as Torah' is a shared-text note.
Trapdoor: 'one Hebrew verb for both plans' refers to ḥashav in Genesis 50:20 (ḥashavtem … ḥashavah). Confirm.
Grace: Pop is home from the hospital and says the fall 'did us a favor'.
